title: 19 — AI / ML Foundations
html:
19 — AI / ML Foundations

Written for a software engineer, not a researcher. The goal is that you can (a) tell whether a problem is an ML problem, (b) read what a data scientist hands you and spot the flaws, (c) understand what a transformer actually does, and (d) ship and operate a model without breaking things.

1. When is a problem an ML problem?

flowchart TD
    A[Problem] --> B{Can you write the rules?}
    B -->|Yes, and they're stable| C[Write the rules.<br/>Simpler, testable, explainable]
    B -->|No — the pattern is in the data| D{Do you have labelled examples,<br/>or a clear signal?}
    D -->|No| E[Get data first, or use<br/>unsupervised/heuristics/an LLM]
    D -->|Yes| F{Is an approximate answer<br/>acceptable?}
    F -->|No, must be exact| C
    F -->|Yes| G{Is the cost of a wrong answer<br/>manageable and detectable?}
    G -->|No| H[Human in the loop,<br/>or don't automate]
    G -->|Yes| I[ML is a reasonable fit]

ML is appropriate when: the rules are too numerous or subtle to write by hand (spam, image content, language), the pattern changes over time (fraud, recommendations), an approximate answer has value, and you can measure whether it's working.

ML is the wrong tool when: rules are known and stable (tax calculation, eligibility criteria), you need exact reproducibility and legal explainability with no exceptions, the cost of an error is catastrophic and undetectable, or you have too little data.

⚠️ The most common mistake in industry: using ML where a WHERE clause and three business rules would do. A rules engine is testable, explainable, debuggable, and doesn't drift. Reach for ML when you've established that rules genuinely don't work.

2. The taxonomy

Paradigm You give it It learns to Examples
Supervised Inputs + correct outputs Predict the output for new inputs Classification (spam/not), regression (price)
Unsupervised Inputs only Find structure Clustering (segments), dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection
Self-supervised Raw data; labels derived from it Predict masked/next parts How LLMs are pre-trained
Reinforcement An environment + reward A policy that maximises reward Game playing, control, RLHF for alignment
Semi-supervised Few labels + lots of unlabelled Leverage both Common when labelling is expensive

Classification vs regression: discrete category vs continuous number. Predicting "will this client churn?" is classification; "how much will they invest?" is regression. Predicting a probability is classification with a calibrated output — and calibration matters enormously if you use the score for a threshold decision.

3. The lifecycle (where projects actually fail)

flowchart LR
    A[Frame the problem<br/>+ define the metric] --> B[Get and understand data]
    B --> C[Split: train / val / test]
    C --> D[Baseline — always]
    D --> E[Features]
    E --> F[Train]
    F --> G[Evaluate on validation]
    G --> H{Good enough vs baseline?}
    H -->|No| E
    H -->|Yes| I[Test set — ONCE]
    I --> J[Ship behind a flag / shadow mode]
    J --> K[Monitor: performance, drift, fairness]
    K --> L[Retrain on a schedule or trigger]
    L --> B

Where projects die, in order of frequency:

  1. The metric doesn't match the business goal. 99% accuracy on a 1%-positive dataset by always predicting "no" is a useless model that looks excellent.
  2. Data leakage — see §5.1. Produces a model that looks brilliant offline and fails in production.
  3. No baseline — you can't tell whether the model adds value over "always predict the mean" or a three-rule heuristic.
  4. Train/serve skew — features computed differently in training and in production.
  5. No monitoring — the model degrades silently as the world changes.

Always build the dumbest possible baseline first: the majority class, the mean, last week's value, or a simple rule. Then the question becomes "is the model worth the complexity?" rather than "does the model work?".

4. Evaluation metrics — get this right or nothing else matters

4.1 Classification

                Predicted
              Pos       Neg
Actual Pos │  TP   │   FN   │  ← missed detections
       Neg │  FP   │   TN   │  ← false alarms
Metric Formula Answers Use when
Accuracy (TP+TN)/all "How often right?" Balanced classes only. Misleading otherwise
Precision TP/(TP+FP) "When I say yes, how often am I right?" False positives are costly (spam filter, auto-blocking)
Recall (sensitivity) TP/(TP+FN) "Of all real positives, how many did I catch?" False negatives are costly (disease, fraud, safety)
F1 harmonic mean of P and R Balance When you need one number and classes are imbalanced
ROC-AUC area under TPR/FPR curve Ranking quality across thresholds Balanced-ish data
PR-AUC area under precision/recall Ranking quality on the positive class Imbalanced data — use this, not ROC-AUC
Log loss / Brier probability error Calibration When you use the score as a probability

The precision/recall trade-off is a business decision, not a modelling one. Moving the threshold trades one for the other. Frame it in money: "at this threshold we catch 80% of fraud and falsely block 2% of legitimate transactions; each false block costs us £X in support and churn."

⚠️ Class imbalance: with 0.1% fraud, accuracy is meaningless and even AUC can flatter. Use PR-AUC, report precision at a fixed recall (or vice versa), and consider resampling/class weights — but note that resampling distorts predicted probabilities, so recalibrate if you use them.

4.2 Regression

Metric Property
MAE Average absolute error; in the units of the target; robust to outliers
RMSE Penalises large errors more; same units; sensitive to outliers
MAPE Percentage error; ⚠️ explodes near zero and is asymmetric
R² Fraction of variance explained; comparable across datasets but easy to misread

4.3 Ranking / recommendation

Precision@k, Recall@k, MAP, NDCG (position-weighted relevance), MRR. Offline metrics correlate imperfectly with business outcomes — A/B test the thing you actually care about (engagement, revenue, retention).

4.4 Splitting data correctly

Situation Split
Independent rows Random 70/15/15
Time series Chronological — train on the past, test on the future. A random split leaks the future
Grouped data (multiple rows per customer) Group split — all of one customer's rows on one side, or you leak identity
Small data k-fold cross-validation
Rare positives Stratified split

The test set is touched once, at the end. Every time you look at it and adjust, you leak information into your model selection and your reported number becomes optimistic. Use the validation set for iteration.

5. Data and features

5.1 Leakage — the defining failure mode

Leakage is any information in your training features that wouldn't be available at prediction time, or that encodes the answer.

Leak Example
Target leakage Using account_closed_date to predict churn
Temporal leakage Computing a feature over the full dataset including the future
Preprocessing leakage Fitting the scaler/imputer on the full dataset before splitting
Duplicate leakage The same record in train and test
Group leakage The same customer in both splits
Metadata leakage Row ordering, ID ranges, or file structure correlating with the label

The tell: results that look too good (99% AUC on a hard problem). The rule: fit every transformation inside the training fold only, and simulate the production timeline exactly.

# ✔ Everything fit inside the pipeline, inside the fold — no leakage
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale",  StandardScaler()),
    ("model",  GradientBoostingClassifier()),
])
scores = cross_val_score(pipeline, X_train, y_train, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="average_precision")

5.2 Feature engineering

Data type Techniques
Numeric Scaling (needed for linear/NN, not for trees), log transform for skew, binning, ratios and differences (often more predictive than raw values)
Categorical One-hot (low cardinality), target/mean encoding (⚠️ leaks badly if not fold-wise), embeddings (high cardinality), ordinal only when genuinely ordered
Datetime Day of week, hour, month, is-holiday, days-since-event, cyclical sin/cos encoding
Text TF-IDF, n-grams, embeddings
Missing Median/mode imputation plus an is_missing indicator — the missingness is often itself signal
Aggregates Rolling counts/sums/means per entity over a window (⚠️ compute with strict as-of semantics)

Feature stores exist to solve train/serve skew: the same feature definition, computed the same way, for both training (point-in-time correct historical values) and serving (fresh values). If you don't use one, at minimum share the feature code between the training pipeline and the inference service.

5.3 Bias/variance and generalisation

Underfitting (high bias)          Good fit             Overfitting (high variance)
train error: high                 train: low           train: very low
test error:  high                 test:  low           test: high  ← memorised the noise
Symptom Fix
Both errors high More capacity, better features, longer training
Train low, test high More data, regularisation (L1/L2, dropout), simpler model, early stopping, augmentation
Both low, production bad Distribution shift or leakage — check §5.1 and §8

Regularisation: L1 (Lasso) drives weights to zero → feature selection; L2 (Ridge) shrinks weights → stability; dropout randomly zeroes activations during training; early stopping halts when validation loss rises.

6. The algorithms worth knowing

Algorithm How it works Strengths Weaknesses
Linear/Logistic regression Weighted sum (+ sigmoid) Fast, interpretable coefficients, calibrated probabilities, a strong baseline Only linear relationships (unless you engineer them)
Decision tree Recursive splits on features Interpretable, handles mixed types, no scaling needed Overfits alone; unstable
Random Forest Many trees on bootstrapped samples, averaged Robust, few knobs, good default Larger, less interpretable
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) Trees fit sequentially to residuals The best off-the-shelf model for tabular data. Wins most competitions Needs tuning; can overfit; slower to train
k-NN Predict from the nearest examples No training, intuitive Slow at inference; suffers in high dimensions
SVM Maximum-margin separator (+ kernels) Effective in high dimensions, small data Doesn't scale to large n; probabilities need calibration
Naive Bayes Bayes with independence assumption Extremely fast, works on tiny data, good for text The independence assumption is usually false
k-means Iteratively assign to nearest centroid Simple, fast clustering Must pick k; assumes spherical clusters
PCA Project onto directions of maximum variance Dimensionality reduction, visualisation Linear; components are hard to interpret
Neural networks Layers of learned nonlinear transforms State of the art on images, text, audio, sequences Needs lots of data and compute; opaque

The practical rule for structured/tabular business data: start with logistic regression as the baseline, then gradient boosting. Deep learning rarely wins on tabular data and costs far more in complexity.

7. Neural networks and transformers

7.1 The basics

A neuron computes activation(w·x + b). Stack them in layers; the network learns the weights.

Training loop:

  1. Forward pass — compute the prediction.
  2. Loss — measure the error (cross-entropy for classification, MSE for regression).
  3. Backpropagation — the chain rule gives the gradient of the loss w.r.t. every weight.
  4. Optimiser step — move the weights against the gradient (SGD, Adam/AdamW).
  5. Repeat over batches and epochs.

Key knobs: learning rate (the single most important), batch size, epochs, architecture depth/width, activation (ReLU/GELU), normalisation (batch/layer norm), and regularisation.

7.2 Architectures

Type Inductive bias Use
MLP None Tabular, final layers of other networks
CNN Local spatial patterns, translation invariance Images, spectrograms, some time series
RNN/LSTM/GRU Sequential, ordered state Sequences (largely superseded by transformers)
Transformer Attention over all positions in parallel Text, code, vision, audio, multimodal — nearly everything now
GNN Graph structure Molecules, social networks, recommendations
Diffusion Iterative denoising Image/audio/video generation

7.3 The transformer, explained properly

The core mechanism is self-attention: every token computes a weighted combination of every other token, where the weights are learned relevance scores.

For each token, project into three vectors:
  Q (query)  = "what am I looking for?"
  K (key)    = "what do I offer?"
  V (value)  = "what do I contribute?"

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √d_k ) · V

 - Q·Kᵀ      → how much each token should attend to each other token
 - / √d_k    → scaling that keeps softmax gradients healthy
 - softmax   → turns scores into weights summing to 1
 - · V       → weighted sum of the value vectors

flowchart TB
    T[Token IDs] --> E[Token embeddings + positional encoding]
    E --> B1["Transformer block × N"]
    subgraph B1
      MHA["Multi-head self-attention<br/>(several attention patterns in parallel)"] --> AN[Add & LayerNorm]
      AN --> FF["Feed-forward network<br/>(per-position MLP)"]
      FF --> AN2[Add & LayerNorm]
    end
    B1 --> OUT["Output head → logits over the vocabulary"]
    OUT --> S[Sampling → next token]

Why it beat RNNs: every position is computed in parallel (RNNs are inherently sequential), and any token can attend directly to any other regardless of distance (no vanishing signal over long ranges).

The cost: attention is O(n²) in sequence length — doubling the context quadruples the compute. This is why long context is expensive and why FlashAttention, sliding-window attention, and similar optimisations exist.

Multi-head attention: several attention computations run in parallel with different learned projections, so different heads can specialise (syntax, coreference, position). Positional encoding: attention itself is order-blind, so position information is injected (sinusoidal, learned, or RoPE — rotary embeddings, now standard). Causal masking: in a decoder (GPT-style), each token may only attend to earlier tokens — that's what makes next-token prediction well-posed.

7.4 How an LLM is built

  1. Pre-training — next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of text. This is where the knowledge and capability come from. Costs millions.
  2. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) — trained on curated instruction/response pairs to become useful rather than merely predictive.
  3. Preference optimisation (RLHF/DPO) — trained on human preference comparisons to be helpful, harmless, and honest.
  4. (Optional) domain fine-tuning — your data, on top of the above.

What this implies practically: the model is a next-token predictor shaped to follow instructions. It has no notion of truth, no access to your data unless you provide it, and no memory between calls unless you supply it. Everything in file 20 follows from those three facts.

8. Production ML (MLOps)

8.1 The extra concerns versus normal software

Concern Why it's different
Versioning Code and data and model and features must all be versioned together to reproduce a result
Train/serve skew The same feature must be computed identically offline and online
Drift The world changes; a static model silently degrades
Non-determinism Same code, different seed/hardware → different model
Silent failure A broken model returns plausible-looking numbers rather than an error
Feedback loops The model's outputs influence future training data (recommendations, fraud rules)

8.2 Deployment patterns

Pattern Latency Use
Batch scoring Hours Scores written to a table, read by the app. Simplest — prefer it whenever the use case allows
Real-time endpoint ms Per-request inference; needs a serving stack and autoscaling
Streaming seconds Score events as they arrive
Edge/on-device ms Privacy, offline, latency
Shadow mode — Run the new model on real traffic, log predictions, take no action. The safest way to validate

8.3 Monitoring

Layer Watch
Service Latency, error rate, throughput, cost per prediction
Input drift Distribution of each feature vs training (PSI, KL divergence, KS test)
Prediction drift Distribution of outputs — a sudden shift usually means an upstream data change
Performance Accuracy/precision/recall against ground truth when labels arrive (often delayed by days/weeks)
Data quality Nulls, ranges, schema, freshness — most "model degradation" is actually a broken feature pipeline
Fairness Metrics sliced by protected attributes, monitored over time

⚠️ Ground truth is usually delayed. For fraud you may not know the true label for 60 days. Design proxy metrics (input drift, prediction distribution, downstream business KPIs) that alert sooner.

8.4 Retraining

Triggers: scheduled (weekly/monthly), drift-threshold breach, or performance drop. Always validate a retrained model against the incumbent on a holdout before promoting it, and keep the ability to roll back to the previous model version instantly. A model registry (MLflow, Azure ML, SageMaker) that tracks lineage, metrics, and stage (staging/production/archived) is the minimum tooling.

8.5 Responsible AI — the engineering obligations

Concern Practice
Bias Measure metrics per demographic slice, not just in aggregate. Bias in the training data becomes bias in the model, and automation scales it
Explainability SHAP/LIME for feature attribution; simpler models where a decision must be justified to a regulator or a customer
Contestability A person affected by an automated decision should be able to see why and challenge it (GDPR Art. 22 for solely-automated significant decisions)
Privacy Minimise PII in features; consider differential privacy; models can memorise and leak training data
Human oversight Keep a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions; define an override path
Documentation Model cards: intended use, training data, performance by slice, known limitations, out-of-scope uses
Security Adversarial inputs, data poisoning, model extraction, membership inference

9. Checklist & interview angles

Before shipping a model

  • Business metric defined, and the ML metric demonstrably correlates with it
  • Baseline built and beaten by a margin that justifies the complexity
  • Split respects time and grouping; test set used once
  • Leakage explicitly checked (feature-by-feature: "would I know this at prediction time?")
  • Feature computation shared between training and serving
  • Performance reported per meaningful slice, not just in aggregate
  • Threshold chosen from a cost analysis, not from the default 0.5
  • Probabilities calibrated if used as probabilities
  • Shadow mode or a canary before full rollout
  • Monitoring: drift, quality, performance-when-labels-arrive
  • Rollback to the previous model version is one action
  • Model, data, code, and features versioned together
  • Fairness assessed; documentation written; human override defined

🔍 Interview angles

  • Why is accuracy a bad metric? Class imbalance — a trivial constant predictor can score 99%. Use precision/recall/PR-AUC and pick the operating point from business cost.
  • What is data leakage and how do you detect it? Information in features that wouldn't exist at prediction time; detected by suspiciously good results, and prevented by fitting all transforms inside the training fold and simulating the production timeline.
  • Explain bias vs variance. Underfitting (too simple, high error everywhere) vs overfitting (memorised noise, gap between train and test).
  • How does self-attention work? Each token emits query, key, and value vectors; softmax over scaled query·key dot products yields weights over all positions; the output is the weighted sum of values. Parallel across positions, O(n²) in length.
  • Why did transformers replace RNNs? Parallel training and direct long-range dependencies without vanishing gradients.
  • How do you know a deployed model is still working? Input and prediction drift monitoring immediately, ground-truth performance when labels arrive, and business KPIs — plus data-quality checks, because most degradation is a broken pipeline, not a stale model.
  • When would you not use ML? Stable known rules, exactness or full explainability required, insufficient data, or undetectable and costly errors.
